However, although people use natural language to reason effectively, it may be that LMs could reason more effectively with some intermediate computation that is not in natural language. In this work, we explore an alternative reasoning approach: instead of explicitly producing the chain of thought reasoning steps, we use the language model's internal hidden states to perform implicit reasoning. The implicit reasoning steps are distilled from a teacher model trained on explicit chain-of-thought reasoning, and instead of doing reasoning "horizontally" by producing intermediate words one-by-one, we distill it such that the reasoning happens "vertically" among the hidden states in different layers. We conduct experiments on a multi-digit multiplication task and a grade school math problem dataset and find that this approach enables solving tasks previously not solvable without explicit chain-of-thought, at a speed comparable to no chain-of-thought.

papers.title: Unveiling Confirmation Bias in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does confirmation bias affect chain-of-thought reasoning behavior in LLMs, and why does its influence vary across questions, reasoning types, and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that confirmation bias is pervasive in LLMs' chain-of-thought reasoning, affecting both reasoning generation and answer prediction, and explains variance in CoT effectiveness across tasks and models.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that confirmation bias significantly impacts CoT reasoning in LLMs, explaining performance variance across tasks and models, and highlights the difficulty of debiasing strong beliefs.
papers.key_findings:
Internal beliefs (approximated by direct QA probabilities) significantly influence CoT performance at both reasoning generation and answer prediction stages.
Questions with stronger beliefs (lower entropy) are more likely to retain correctness regardless of difficulty, showing confirmation bias.
CoT improvement aligns with the degree to which tasks are prone to confirmation bias, with greater improvement on symbolic reasoning (e.g., math) than on non-symbolic tasks.
Models with weaker beliefs (higher entropy) are more sensitive to the quality and structure of the generated rationale.
Debiasing internal beliefs is challenging, especially when beliefs are strong, as models struggle to follow rationales that contradict their confident prior beliefs.
papers.limitation: The use of entropy as a proxy for belief strength limits analysis to white-box LLMs and multiple-choice questions.
future_direction: Explore confirmation bias using confidence measures applicable to black-box LLMs and open-ended questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been widely adopted to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).However, the effectiveness of CoT reasoning is inconsistent across tasks with different reasoning types.This work presents a novel perspective to understand CoT behavior through the lens of confirmation bias in cognitive psychology.Specifically, we examine how model internal beliefs, approximated by direct questionanswering probabilities, affect both reasoning generation (Q R) and reasoning-guided answer prediction (QR A) in CoT.By decomposing CoT into a two-stage process, we conduct a thorough correlation analysis in model beliefs, rationale attributes, and stage-wise performance.Our results provide strong evidence of confirmation bias in LLMs, such that model beliefs not only skew the reasoning process but also influence how rationales are utilized for answer prediction.Furthermore, the interplay between task vulnerability to confirmation bias and the strength of beliefs also provides explanations for CoT effectiveness across reasoning tasks and models.Overall, this study provides a valuable insight for the needs of better prompting strategies that mitigate confirmation bias to enhance reasoning performance.Code is available at https://github.com/yuewan2/biasedcot.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought, and what factors affect faithful versus unfaithful recovery?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs have two distinct modes of reasoning (faithful and unfaithful) when recovering from errors in chain-of-thought, and these modes respond differently to factors like error magnitude and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have two distinct reasoning modes: one faithful and interpretable, and one unfaithful where the generated text does not accurately represent the internal reasoning. This challenges the reliability of chain-of-thought for model auditing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs recover more frequently from larger errors than smaller ones.
Prior expectations of errors (via context noise or prompting) increase error recovery rates.
More evidence for the correct value in the context increases error recovery rates.
Faithful and unfaithful recoveries respond differently to interventions, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Different models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3) show varying patterns in faithful vs. unfaithful recovery.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to mathematical reasoning problems and does not investigate non-mathematical reasoning errors; additionally, the introduced errors may differ from naturally occurring errors.
future_direction: Understanding the mechanisms underlying faithful and unfaithful reasoning modes
Identifying factors that influence which reasoning mode is activated
Developing techniques to encourage faithful reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often improve their performance in downstream tasks when they generate Chain of Thought reasoning text before producing an answer. We investigate how LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought. Through analysis of error recovery behaviors, we find evidence for unfaithfulness in Chain of Thought, which occurs when models arrive at the correct answer despite invalid reasoning text. We identify factors that shift LLM recovery behavior: LLMs recover more frequently from obvious errors and in contexts that provide more evidence for the correct answer. Critically, these factors have divergent effects on faithful and unfaithful recoveries. Our results indicate that there are distinct mechanisms driving faithful and unfaithful error recoveries. Selective targeting of these mechanisms may be able to drive down the rate of unfaithful reasoning and improve model interpretability.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting: An Empirical Study of What Matters
papers.research_question: What makes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance? Specifically, are ground truth bridging objects/language templates important, and if not, what are the key aspects needed for the LLM to reason properly?
papers.core_contribution: The validity of reasoning in Chain-of-Thought demonstrations is not crucial for performance; instead, the relevance of the rationale to the query and the coherence (correct ordering) of the reasoning steps are the key aspects that determine the effectiveness of CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: The study deepens understanding of CoT prompting by showing that valid reasoning in demonstrations is not the primary driver of performance; instead, relevance and coherence are critical. This suggests LLMs' reasoning abilities largely come from pretraining, and CoT demonstrations mainly regularize the output format.
papers.key_findings:
Providing demonstrations with completely invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance of standard CoT prompting, indicating that logical validity in the examples is not essential.
Relevance (the rationale being based on the query) and coherence (the correct ordering of steps) are identified as the two key aspects for effective CoT prompting.
Relevance is more important than coherence for bridging objects (e.g., numbers, entities), while coherence of language templates is particularly important.
When both relevance and coherence are removed, performance drops significantly, sometimes below standard prompting without rationales.
The findings suggest LLMs may not be learning to reason from the demonstrations but rather using pretrained abilities, with CoT mainly specifying an output format that regularizes generation to be step-by-step, in order, and relevant.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to two types of reasoning tasks (arithmetic reasoning and multi-hop question answering); other tasks like symbolic reasoning were not studied due to their highly template-based nature.
The construction of invalid reasoning demonstrations was done manually, lacking a systematic treatment; automatically synthesizing such rationales is challenging.
Intrinsic evaluation relies on the correctness of bridging objects, which may not be a comprehensive metric and requires costly annotation.
future_direction: Extending the ablation designs to other types of reasoning tasks, such as symbolic reasoning tasks where steps have little variation.
Developing a more systematic treatment of the 'invalid reasoning' setting, e.g., by categorizing informal logical fallacies.
Improving intrinsic evaluation methods to be more comprehensive and reference-free.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting can dramatically improve the multi-step reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). CoT explicitly encourages the LLM to generate intermediate rationales for solving a problem, by providing a series of reasoning steps in the demonstrations. Despite its success, there is still little understanding of what makes CoT prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance. In this paper, we show that CoT reasoning is possible even with invalid demonstrations - prompting with invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance obtained using CoT under various metrics, while still generating coherent lines of reasoning during inference. Further experiments show that other aspects of the rationales, such as being relevant to the query and correctly ordering the reasoning steps, are much more important for effective CoT reasoning. Overall, these findings both deepen our understanding of CoT prompting, and open up new questions regarding LLMs' capability to learn to reason in context.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
papers.research_question: Which reasoning steps (sentences) in a chain-of-thought are important for guiding the reasoning trajectory and final answer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sentence-level analysis methods (black-box resampling and white-box attention analysis) to identify 'thought anchors'—critical reasoning steps that guide the trajectory of chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Sentence-level analysis provides a promising intermediate abstraction for understanding reasoning in LLMs, with methods converging to identify critical 'thought anchor' steps that structure the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
Plan generation and uncertainty management sentences have higher counterfactual importance than active computation or fact retrieval sentences.
Specialized 'receiver' attention heads consistently attend to thought anchor sentences, providing a mechanistic correlate of importance.
Sentence-sentence causal graphs reveal that stronger close-range links and weaker long-range links correlate with higher reasoning accuracy, especially in mathematical domains.
papers.limitation: The counterfactual importance metric can yield high-variance estimates when the number of semantically divergent resampled sentences is low.
future_direction: Investigating adaptive scales for defining reasoning steps beyond fixed sentences.
Further work on the limitations of the counterfactual importance metric with limited data.
papers.abstract: Current frontier large-language models rely on reasoning to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Many existing interpretability are limited in this area, as standard methods have been designed to study single forward passes of a model rather than the multi-token computational steps that unfold during reasoning. We argue that analyzing reasoning traces at the sentence level is a promising approach to understanding reasoning processes. We introduce a black-box method that measures each sentence's counterfactual importance by repeatedly sampling replacement sentences from the model, filtering for semantically different ones, and continuing the chain of thought from that point onwards to quantify the sentence's impact on the distribution of final answers. We discover that certain sentences can have an outsized impact on the trajectory of the reasoning trace and final answer. We term these sentences \textit{thought anchors}. These are generally planning or uncertainty management sentences, and specialized attention heads consistently attend from subsequent sentences to thought anchors. We further show that examining sentence-sentence causal links within a reasoning trace gives insight into a model's behavior. Such information can be used to predict a problem's difficulty and the extent different question domains involve sequential or diffuse reasoning. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate that our techniques together provide a practical toolkit for analyzing reasoning models by conducting a detailed case study of how the model solves a difficult math problem, finding that our techniques yield a consistent picture of the reasoning trace's structure. We provide an open-source tool (thought-anchors.com) for visualizing the outputs of our methods on further problems. The convergence across our methods shows the potential of sentence-level analysis for a deeper understanding of reasoning models.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models: Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting in large language models? Specifically, does the model merely mimic exemplars, what changes occur in the projection space (logits), and does CoT enable deeper and broader utilization of pre-trained knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This work analyzes the internal mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting, finding that LLMs imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with question understanding, exhibit fluctuating but ultimately more concentrated logits distributions, and activate a broader set of neurons in final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought prompting enhances LLM reasoning by guiding models to imitate exemplar formats, focus logits distributions, and activate a broader set of knowledge-related neurons, leading to more accurate and confident answers.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs imitate the format of CoT exemplars (e.g., using sequence words like 'first', 'then') while generating personalized responses based on their understanding of the question.
During CoT generation, token logits fluctuate more than with standard prompts, but the final answer generation shows a more concentrated logits distribution, suggesting clearer direction.
CoT prompts lead to a broader range and higher intensity of neuron activations in the final layers compared to standard prompts, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval from pre-training.
Successful imitation of transferred CoT prompts correlates with higher answer accuracy, suggesting that understanding the exemplar format is key to CoT's effectiveness.
The probability distribution over candidate answers at the answer generation step is more concentrated (lower entropy) under CoT prompting, indicating higher model confidence in the selected answer.
papers.limitation: Experiments were conducted on a limited sample of 50 test examples per dataset due to budget constraints.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more models and tasks.
Explore the dynamic changes in neuron activations across different layers.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models, with numerous studies exploring factors influencing its performance. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. To further demystify the operational principles, this work examines three key aspects: decoding, projection, and activation, aiming to elucidate the changes that occur within models when employing Chainof-Thought. Our findings reveal that LLMs effectively imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with their understanding of the question, exhibiting fluctuations in token logits during generation but ultimately producing a more concentrated logits distribution, and activating a broader set of neurons in the final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval compared to standard prompts. Our code and data will be publicly avialable when the paper is accepted.

papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong generalization across a wide range of tasks. Reasoning with LLMs is central to solving multi-step problems and complex decision-making. To support efficient reasoning, recent studies have shifted attention from explicit chain-of-thought prompting toward implicit reasoning, where reasoning occurs silently via latent structures without emitting intermediate textual steps. Implicit reasoning brings advantages such as lower generation cost, faster inference, and better alignment with internal computation. Although prior surveys have discussed latent representations in the context of reasoning, a dedicated and mechanism-level examination of how reasoning unfolds internally within LLMs remains absent. This survey fills that gap by introducing a taxonomy centered on execution paradigms, shifting the focus from representational forms to computational strategies. We organize existing methods into three execution paradigms based on \textbf{\textit{how and where internal computation unfolds}}: latent optimization, signal-guided control, and layer-recurrent execution. We also review structural, behavioral and representation-based evidence that supports the presence of implicit reasoning in LLMs. We further provide a structured overview of the evaluation metrics and benchmarks used in existing works to assess the effectiveness and reliability of implicit reasoning. We maintain a continuously updated project at: https://github.com/digailab/awesome-llm-implicit-reasoning.

papers.title: Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: Does Huginn exhibit signs of latent chain-of-thought reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: We find limited evidence of interpretable latent chain-of-thought reasoning in the depth-recurrent transformer Huginn-3.5B, and uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks.
papers.conclusion: We find little evidence of structured latent chain-of-thought reasoning in Huginn, but it may be more subtle or distributed than our tools can detect.
papers.key_findings:
Probing inconsistencies across blocks in Huginn's depth-recurrent architecture: hidden state interpretability depends heavily on block index and decoding method.
Token rank trajectory analysis provides little evidence for latent CoT reasoning.
Scaling recurrence depth fails to match explicit reasoning: increasing recurrent steps only marginally improves performance and falls short of explicit CoT prompting.
papers.limitation: The results do not definitively rule out the presence of latent CoT; it may be more subtle or distributed than our employed tools can detect.
future_direction: Apply more advanced probing techniques, such as activation patching, to uncover finer-grained reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has enabled transformer-based language models to excel at complex mathematics and multi-step planning. However, in standard decoder-only architectures, these reasoning steps are externalized in natural language, improving interpretability at the cost of efficiency. To capture reasoning that is not easily represented in words, many works have explored recurrent architectures that aim to internalize reasoning in latent space, potentially supporting latent CoT. In this paper, we investigate whether such reasoning structures emerge in Huginn-3.5B, a depth-recurrent Transformer that reuses layers at inference time without increasing parameter count. We examine the model's internal behavior on arithmetic tasks using a suite of probing techniques including the Logit Lens and Coda Lens. Our findings reveal limited evidence of interpretable latent CoT by tracking rank trajectories of final and intermediate result tokens. Furthermore, we uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks, where the interpretability of hidden states depends heavily on both the layer index and the decoding method. Finally, we empirically show that increasing recurrence depth yields only marginal gains and falls well short of models that explicitly externalize reasoning steps. The code is available at https://github.com/wenquanlu/huginn-latent-cot.

papers.title: Semantic Composition in Visually Grounded Language Models
papers.research_question: This thesis explores whether and how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces multiple methods (WinogroundVQA, Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, Causal Tracing, Syntactic MeanPool, Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization) to probe, analyze, and improve the compositional abilities of visually grounded language models.
papers.conclusion: The work explores the compositionality of visually grounded semantics, introducing methods to probe and improve it, and draws connections to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.
papers.key_findings:
Generative vision-language models like BLIP 2.0 and MiniGPT-4 perform poorly on the compositional WinogroundVQA benchmark.
Syntactic Neural Module Distillation reveals that larger sentence embedding models (GTR-T5) are more compositional, but model size is not the only determining factor.
Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization (CACR) improves relation alignment in vision-language models and outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method (IAIS) on the Winoground benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, hyperparameter tuning for the SynNaMoN experiments was unfeasible, and the dataset had to be constrained to a subset of trees and production rules.
The choice of linguistic formalism (Penn Treebank) may influence the probing results of compositional structure.
future_direction: Exploring whether different linguistic formalisms are better proxies for a model's compositional structure.
Further work on the causal tracing experiment for image captioning models (implementation in progress).
papers.abstract: What is sentence meaning and its ideal representation? Much of the expressive power of human language derives from semantic composition, the mind's ability to represent meaning hierarchically & relationally over constituents. At the same time, much sentential meaning is outside the text and requires grounding in sensory, motor, and experiential modalities to be adequately learned. Although large language models display considerable compositional ability, recent work shows that visually-grounded language models drastically fail to represent compositional structure. In this thesis, we explore whether & how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so. Specifically, we introduce 1) WinogroundVQA, a new compositional visual question answering benchmark, 2) Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, a measure of compositional ability in sentence embedding models, 3) Causal Tracing for Image Captioning Models to locate neural representations vital for vision-language composition, 4) Syntactic MeanPool to inject a compositional inductive bias into sentence embeddings, and 5) Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization, a self-supervised objective function for vision-language relation alignment. We close by discussing connections of our work to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.

papers.title: Efficient Post-Training Refinement of Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to effectively update reasoning embeddings during post-training to guide the model toward more accurate solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight post-training framework that refines latent reasoning trajectories using contrastive feedback and residual embedding refinement, improving reasoning accuracy without additional training.
papers.conclusion: The proposed latent reasoning framework with residual refinement and contrastive search improves reasoning accuracy across multiple benchmarks without retraining, demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves accuracy over latent-only reasoning (Coconut) and explicit token-based reasoning (CoT) on four out of five tasks, with gains of up to 5% on MathQA.
The method is training-free and adds minimal overhead during inference, making it efficient.
Both residual refinement and contrastive search contribute to performance improvement, with residual refinement providing stability and contrastive search enabling error correction.
The method generalizes across different model architectures (GPT-2, Qwen, LLaMA) and sizes.
Latent reasoning reduces token usage by over 92% compared to CoT, making it more cost-efficient.
papers.limitation:
Tested only on relatively small LLMs, not comparable to latest models like ChatGPT-4.1 or DeepSeek-R1.
Does not compare with sampling-based or search-based CoT variants.
Latent reasoning may not be optimal for all tasks, e.g., math problems that require explicit written logic.
Latent reasoning lacks human-readable intermediate steps, making interpretation harder.
future_direction: Apply routing method to dynamically reason the query
Introduce tools to enhance reasoning processes
papers.abstract: Reasoning is a key component of language understanding in Large Language Models. While Chain-of-Thought prompting enhances performance via explicit intermediate steps, it suffers from sufficient token overhead and a fixed reasoning trajectory, preventing step-wise refinement. Recent advances in latent reasoning address these limitations by refining internal reasoning processes directly in the model's latent space, without producing explicit outputs. However, a key challenge remains: how to effectively update reasoning embeddings during post-training to guide the model toward more accurate solutions. To overcome this challenge, we propose a lightweight post-training framework that refines latent reasoning trajectories using two novel strategies: 1) Contrastive reasoning feedback, which compares reasoning embeddings against strong and weak baselines to infer effective update directions via embedding enhancement; 2) Residual embedding refinement, which stabilizes updates by progressively integrating current and historical gradients, enabling fast yet controlled convergence. Extensive experiments and case studies are conducted on five reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Notably, a 5\% accuracy gain on MathQA without additional training.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Is Chain-of-Thought Really Not Explainability? Chain-of-Thought Can Be Faithful without Hint Verbalization
papers.research_question: Does the Biasing Features metric overstate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) unfaithfulness by conflating it with incompleteness, and can CoTs be faithful without explicitly verbalizing hints?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the Biasing Features metric overstates CoT unfaithfulness by conflating it with incompleteness, and shows through the faithful@k metric and causal mediation analysis that CoTs can be faithful without explicitly verbalizing hints.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that claims of widespread CoT unfaithfulness are overstated due to over-reliance on the Biasing Features metric, and advocates for using multiple metrics and causal mediation analysis to assess CoT faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoTs flagged as unfaithful by Biasing Features are often faithful under other metrics (e.g., Filler Tokens and FUR).
Much of the measured unfaithfulness is better attributed to incompleteness; with larger inference-time budgets, hint verbalization increases (up to 90% in some settings).
Even when CoTs do not verbalize hints, they can causally mediate part of the hints' influence on model predictions (non-zero indirect effect).
CoTs can shift predictions by decreasing the probability of non-hinted options, not only by increasing the hinted option.
The Biasing Features metric is better seen as a test of verbalized sensitivity rather than faithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Experiments do not include larger models or specialized reasoning models due to computational constraints.
FUR experiments are memory intensive and faithful@k analysis requires generating many samples and LLM-as-judge evaluation, which are expensive.
future_direction: Improve CoTs by encouraging models to expose implicit, real-world factors through broader, more generalizable objectives, rather than optimizing for verbalizing toy interventions.
papers.abstract: Recent work, using the Biasing Features metric, labels a CoT as unfaithful if it omits a prompt-injected hint that affected the prediction. We argue this metric confuses unfaithfulness with incompleteness, the lossy compression needed to turn distributed transformer computation into a linear natural language narrative. On multi-hop reasoning tasks with Llama-3 and Gemma-3, many CoTs flagged as unfaithful by Biasing Features are judged faithful by other metrics, exceeding 50% in some models. With a new faithful@k metric, we show that larger inference-time token budgets greatly increase hint verbalization (up to 90% in some settings), suggesting much apparent unfaithfulness is due to tight token limits. Using Causal Mediation Analysis, we further show that even non-verbalized hints can causally mediate prediction changes through the CoT. We therefore caution against relying solely on hint-based evaluations and advocate a broader interpretability toolkit, including causal mediation and corruption-based metrics.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the language model perform multi-step reasoning by recalling memorized information or by following a step-by-step reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that language models perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning tree information can often be detected from attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that encode reasoning information degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with better accuracy and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The work considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
Analysis of multi-head attention is limited; shallow models with many heads might have different head functions.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that language models (LMs) have strong multi-step (i.e., procedural) reasoning capabilities. However, it is unclear whether LMs perform these tasks by cheating with answers memorized from pretraining corpus, or, via a multi-step reasoning mechanism. In this paper, we try to answer this question by exploring a mechanistic interpretation of LMs for multi-step reasoning tasks. Concretely, we hypothesize that the LM implicitly embeds a reasoning tree resembling the correct reasoning process within it. We test this hypothesis by introducing a new probing approach (called MechanisticProbe) that recovers the reasoning tree from the model's attention patterns. We use our probe to analyze two LMs: GPT-2 on a synthetic task (k-th smallest element), and LLaMA on two simple language-based reasoning tasks (ProofWriter & AI2 Reasoning Challenge). We show that MechanisticProbe is able to detect the information of the reasoning tree from the model's attentions for most examples, suggesting that the LM indeed is going through a process of multi-step reasoning within its architecture in many cases.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Explainable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: An Empirical Analysis on State-Aware Reasoning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we abstract and model the latent structure of chain-of-thought reasoning to provide a global, explainable view of reasoning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a state-aware transition framework that abstracts chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories into structured latent dynamics via spectral analysis and Markov chains, enabling a global, explainable view of reasoning steps and transitions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a global perspective on multi-step reasoning in LLMs, uncovering consistent latent structures across models and tasks, and enables explainability applications for CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully abstracts CoT reasoning steps into semantically coherent latent states via spectral embeddings and clustering.
Learned transition patterns are consistent across models and tasks, indicating structured reasoning dynamics beyond surface token sequences.
The latent states correspond to meaningful functional roles (e.g., scenario description, problem framing, answer synthesis).
The Markov chain model captures coherent temporal reasoning flows, validated by Monte Carlo simulations.
The approach enables explainability applications such as semantic role identification and temporal pattern visualization.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes access to internal representations of open-source language models.
It focuses primarily on intrinsic structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting have enabled large language models (LLMs) to perform multi-step reasoning. However, the explainability of such reasoning remains limited, with prior work primarily focusing on local token-level attribution, such that the high-level semantic roles of reasoning steps and their transitions remain underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a state-aware transition framework that abstracts CoT trajectories into structured latent dynamics. Specifically, to capture the evolving semantics of CoT reasoning, each reasoning step is represented via spectral analysis of token-level embeddings and clustered into semantically coherent latent states. To characterize the global structure of reasoning, we model their progression as a Markov chain, yielding a structured and interpretable view of the reasoning process. This abstraction supports a range of analyses, including semantic role identification, temporal pattern visualization, and consistency evaluation.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Unveiling Internal Reasoning Modes in LLMs: A Deep Dive into Latent Reasoning vs. Factual Shortcuts with Attribute Rate Ratio
papers.research_question: How do latent reasoning and factual shortcuts differ during inference in LLMs for multi-hop questions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) metric to efficiently distinguish between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts in LLMs, and provides an analysis of internal mechanisms showing that latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate steps.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically investigates distinctions between latent reasoning and factual shortcuts, proposes the ARR metric for efficient classification, and demonstrates its application in RAG conflict scenarios, deepening understanding of model reasoning pathways.
papers.key_findings:
Subject representations differ significantly between reasoning modes: latent reasoning encodes bridge-related information for final answer extraction, while factual shortcuts bypass intermediate reasoning and resemble single-hop factual queries.
The proposed Attribute Rate Ratio (ARR) achieves around 90% accuracy in classifying reasoning modes on constructed datasets.
Model behavior under conflicting prompts in RAG scenarios is closely tied to its underlying reasoning mode, with latent reasoning more influenced by external context and factual shortcuts more robust to disruptive information.
The model undergoes two disjointed stages during multi-hop reasoning: local shallow reasoning (encoding relation-related attributes) and deep reasoning (integrating information for final answer).
Bridge-related information propagated from the subject position plays a decisive role in second-hop reasoning for latent reasoning modes.
papers.limitation:
Scope limited to two-hop reasoning, which may not generalize to more complex reasoning chains.
Limited dataset availability for studying latent reasoning due to many shortcut mappings in training data.
Latent multi-hop reasoning pathway identification relies on CoT filtering, which may not fully correspond to the model's internal reasoning processes.
The proposed metric lacks rigorous verification due to model complexity and limited datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex reasoning beyond two-hop tasks.
Further refinement and verification of the ARR metric.
Investigating the balance between external information utilization and robustness in RAG conflicts.
papers.abstract: Yiran Yang, Haifeng Sun, Jingyu Wang, Qi Qi, Zirui Zhuang, Huazheng Wang, Pengfei Ren, Jing Wang, Jianxin Liao. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Mapping Faithful Reasoning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) traces promise transparency for reasoning language models, but prior work shows they are not always faithful reflections of internal computation. This raises challenges for oversight: practitioners may misinterpret decorative reasoning as genuine. We introduce Concept Walk, a general framework for tracing how a model's internal stance evolves with respect to a concept direction during reasoning. Unlike surface text, Concept Walk operates in activation space, projecting each reasoning step onto the concept direction learned from contrastive data. This allows us to observe whether reasoning traces shape outcomes or are discarded. As a case study, we apply Concept Walk to the domain of Safety using Qwen 3-4B. We find that in 'easy' cases, perturbed CoTs are quickly ignored, indicating decorative reasoning, whereas in 'hard' cases, perturbations induce sustained shifts in internal activations, consistent with faithful reasoning. The contribution is methodological: Concept Walk provides a lens to re-examine faithfulness through concept-specific internal dynamics, helping identify when reasoning traces can be trusted and when they risk misleading practitioners.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.
